title: Clinical Mastery: Brown Syndrome vs. Inferior Oblique (IO) Palsy
summary: Differential diagnosis of vertical strabismus in primary gaze is a classic board challenge. This guide delineates the mechanical restriction of Brown Syndrome from the neurogenic deficit of IO palsy.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Brown Syndrome is a restrictive ocular motility disorder characterized by a limited ability to elevate the adducted eye. Inferior Oblique (IO) Palsy is a cyclovertical muscle paresis leading to primary gaze hypertropia and limited elevation in adduction due to innervation failure.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Perform Cover-Uncover Test to confirm vertical deviation.
Step 2: Assess Ductions and Versions specifically in adduction.
Step 3: Perform Forced Duction Test (FDT) under topical anesthesia to rule out mechanical restriction.
Step 4: Execute Three-Step (Park-Bielschowsky) Test to confirm paretic muscle.
Step 5: Imaging (CT/MRI) if suspected orbital pathology or restrictive trauma.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden onset in adulthood (Rule out tumor/myasthenia)
Evidence of orbital floor blowout fracture

content.explanation: H (Hyper in which eye?), I (In which gaze is it worse?), R/L (Right/Left head tilt test: Head tilt to the same side increases hyper in superior oblique palsy, opposite in IO).

sections.title: Treatment Protocols
content: Brown Syndrome: Observation for mild cases. Surgical management (SO tenectomy/lengthening) only for significant chin-up posture or severe orthotropic limitation.
IO Palsy: Treat underlying cause if paretic. Surgical recession of the contralateral superior rectus or ipsilateral inferior oblique myectomy if persistent binocular diplopia.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Brown Syndrome is characterized by a 'click' on forced duction if it is the clicking type (congenital).
Inferior oblique palsy is rarely isolated; always rule out ipsilateral SO overaction or contralateral SR palsy.
The FDT is the gold standard for distinguishing restrictive versus paretic etiologies.
